scenes.name: S01 The internet behind the screen

lines.text: I'm opening YouTube. What happens behind the scenes?
Every time you open a website, watch a video, or send a message, something interesting happens behind the screen.
Your data travels across networks in the form of packets.
But how do we know what's actually moving through our network?

scenes.name: S02 What is a network packet

lines.text: Think of a network packet as a digital envelope.
It contains information about where it came from, where it's going, how it should be delivered, and the actual data being transmitted.
Open it up, and you'll find layers.
The Ethernet header carries the hardware addresses for this hop on the local network.
The IP header holds the source and destination addresses.
The TCP header adds port numbers, and keeps the conversation in order.
And at the centre is the payload. The actual application data.
A firewall can see where a packet is going. But not always what it is.
A traditional firewall primarily evaluates packet headers and configured policies.
Here, it sees a connection to port four four three. Secure web traffic, but from which application?
Our Deep Packet Inspection Engine goes further.
It analyzes packet structure and supported application-layer information, to identify the traffic and apply intelligent filtering rules.
We capture traffic with a tool like Wireshark, and save it as a PCAP file. The engine works on that recording, one packet at a time.

Our DPI Engine takes captured network traffic as input, processes each packet, identifies supported applications, checks configured blocking rules, and produces filtered traffic, along with a detailed processing report.
Your browser generates network traffic. Our DPI Engine analyzes the packets to understand the connection.
Every packet enters through the PCAP Reader.
It reads the file's global header, then each packet's record header, with its timestamp and length, followed by the raw packet bytes.
The Packet Parser extracts the network information.
MAC addresses from Ethernet. IP addresses and the protocol from IPv4. And port numbers from TCP or UDP.
The engine then uses five important values, known as the Five-Tuple, to identify and track a connection.
Source IP. Destination IP. Source port. Destination port. And protocol.
Every packet with the same five values belongs to the same flow.
Before a browser and a server exchange encrypted data, they perform a TLS handshake. The browser speaks first, with a Client Hello.
Even though HTTPS encrypts application data, a conventional TLS Client Hello may expose the requested hostname, through the Server Name Indication extension.
Our DPI Engine searches for this information, and maps recognized domains to application types.
The engine never decrypts anything. Everything after the handshake stays unreadable.
SNI extraction needs a complete, parsable Client Hello. And when the name is concealed by Encrypted Client Hello, there is no hostname to read.
For unencrypted web traffic, the engine reads the HTTP Host header instead.
Once the hostname is extracted, the engine compares it against known application signatures.
This allows the system to classify recognizable traffic into application categories.
Traffic it cannot recognize is simply labelled unknown. And the result is stored on the flow, for every packet that follows.
Once the application is identified, we can apply the configured network policies.
The engine evaluates traffic against configured IP, application, and domain rules.
When a flow is identified as blocked, the engine marks that connection as blocked, and drops subsequent packets belonging to that flow.
Notice the timing. The handshake packets were already forwarded, because the application was not known yet. Blocking begins once the flow is identified.
To handle larger captures efficiently, the multithreaded version introduces parallel processing.
A Reader thread pulls packets from the file, and Load Balancers distribute them across Fast Path threads.
Consistent hashing ensures that packets belonging to the same connection reach the same processing thread, allowing the engine to maintain flow state.
Hash the Five-Tuple, and the same connection always lands on the same thread.
Between the stages sit thread-safe queues. A producer pushes packets in, and a consumer takes them out.
A mutex guards the queue, and a condition variable wakes the consumer when work arrives.
Finally, the Output Writer thread collects the results.
After processing, the engine writes allowed packets into a filtered PCAP file.
And it generates a report containing packet statistics, application breakdowns, detected domains, and thread-level processing information.
Everything we forwarded, and everything we dropped, is accounted for.
So, this is our Deep Packet Inspection Engine.
It reads captured network traffic, understands packet structures, identifies supported applications, tracks connections, applies blocking rules, and produces filtered traffic with detailed reports.
It's not just about seeing packets. It's about understanding the traffic moving through a network.
